easy.explanation: Verse 1 identifies the vision as belonging to Isaiah the son of Amoz.
easy.q: Who is named as the one who saw the vision?

easy.explanation: The vision concerned Judah and Jerusalem.
easy.q: Concerning which places was the vision given?

easy.explanation: Isaiah calls the heavens and the earth to hear the Lord’s word.
easy.q: Who is called to hear the word of the Lord?

answers: He had nourished and brought them up
He had punished and cast them away
He had sent them to another land
medium.explanation: The Lord says, “I have nourished and brought up children.”
medium.q: What had the Lord done for those He called His children?

answers: They asked the Lord for help
medium.explanation: To rebel against the Lord means to resist or turn away from Him.
medium.q: What does “they have rebelled against me” mean?

answers: Even animals know their masters, but Israel did not know the Lord
medium.explanation: The ox knows its owner and the ass its master’s crib, but Israel does not know its Lord.
medium.q: What does the comparison with the ox and the ass show?

answers: It presents them as witnesses to the Lord’s words
It shows that the prophecy was written outdoors
challenge.explanation: The heavens and earth are summoned to hear, making them witnesses to the accusation.
challenge.q: Why does the call to the heavens and the earth strengthen the prophet’s rebuke?

answers: The Lord raised them up, but they rebelled against Him
The Lord did not know them, but they knew Him
The Lord punished them, but they praised Him
challenge.explanation: The Lord’s care and raising of Israel stand against Israel’s rebellion and departure.
challenge.q: What is the chief contrast between the Lord’s treatment of Israel and Israel’s response?

answers: Israel turned away from the Lord despite the relationship and goodness it received
Israel only wished to leave its land
Israel returned to the Lord in repentance
challenge.explanation: These verses present Israel’s relationship with the Lord and its faithless turning away.

paragraphs.title: The Wounded and Neglected People and Land

easy.explanation: The people are described as having wounds, bruises, and putrifying sores.
easy.q: How is the physical condition of the people described?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “your cities are burned with fire.”
easy.q: What happened to the cities of the land?

easy.explanation: The daughter of Zion was left like a cottage, lodge, or besieged city—isolated and vulnerable.
easy.q: What was left of the daughter of Zion?

answers: It shows that the land also suffered and was ruined
It shows that the people moved to another land
It proves that the land was especially fruitful
medium.explanation: Both the people and the land are portrayed as wounded, ruined, and neglected.
medium.q: What does the description of the land add to the description of the people?

answers: There is no health or wholeness in it
There is great wealth in it
There is great joy in it
medium.explanation: The phrase means that no part of the body was whole or healthy.
medium.q: What does “there is no soundness in it” mean in context?

answers: They both describe prosperity and safety
They both describe destruction and isolation
They both describe a national celebration
medium.explanation: The cities are ruined, and Zion is left alone and exposed.
medium.q: What do the burned cities and the daughter of Zion have in common?

answers: The condition remained neglected and unhealed
The people were not injured at all
challenge.explanation: The lack of treatment emphasizes continued neglect and the absence of healing.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the wounds that were neither closed nor bound up?

answers: To show that some survivors remained after the destruction
To announce that the whole land was full of life
challenge.explanation: Without the Lord’s remnant, the people would have been like Sodom and Gomorrah.
challenge.q: Why is a very small remnant mentioned in verse 9?

challenge.explanation: The comparison indicates that the destruction was nearly complete and extremely severe.
challenge.q: What does the comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah emphasize?

easy.explanation: Isaiah addresses the rulers of Sodom and the people of Gomorrah as a comparison to Judah.
easy.q: To whom does the prophet compare the people?

easy.explanation: The passage mentions sacrifices, burnt offerings, oblations, and incense.
easy.q: What did the people bring in abundance to the Lord?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “when ye make many prayers, I will not hear.”
easy.q: What does the Lord do when the people make many prayers?

answers: The worship was joined to sin and a lack of moral reform
The people did not come to the Temple
medium.explanation: The problem was not merely the offerings, but worship joined to iniquity and injustice.
medium.q: Why does the Lord reject the sacrifices and appointed feasts?

answers: To enter the Lord’s courts without a sincere desire to change
medium.explanation: The phrase portrays outward worship as unwelcome when it is accompanied by wrongdoing.
medium.q: What does “to tread my courts” mean in context?

answers: They are rejected when separated from righteousness
They are accepted in every condition
medium.explanation: The Lord rejects worship that is offered while the people continue in evil.
medium.q: What do the sacrifices, appointed feasts, and prayers have in common in this passage?

answers: More worship does not please Him when evil remains
The Lord asks for still more worship
Worship is not mentioned at all
challenge.explanation: Many offerings and prayers are useless when the people refuse moral correction.
challenge.q: What is the contrast between the abundance of worship and the Lord’s response?

answers: The worshippers are free from sin
The worship is accompanied by serious wrongdoing
challenge.explanation: Blood-filled hands represent the violence and injustice that prevent the worship from being accepted.
challenge.q: What does “your hands are full of blood” signify in the context of prayer?

answers: Outward worship cannot replace righteous conduct
challenge.explanation: The passage teaches that worship without moral reform is unacceptable to the Lord.
challenge.q: What conclusion follows from the criticism of the people’s worship?

answers: Wash, become clean, and stop doing evil
easy.explanation: Isaiah says, “Wash you, make you clean” and “cease to do evil.”
easy.q: What does the prophet first call the people to do?

easy.explanation: They are told to judge the fatherless and plead for the widow.
easy.q: For whom are the people commanded to seek justice?

answers: They shall eat the good of the land
They will live in the wilderness
easy.explanation: The Lord promises, “ye shall eat the good of the land.”
easy.q: What will happen if the people are willing and obedient?

answers: Do evil, then ask for justice
Become clean, stop doing evil, learn to do well, and seek justice
medium.explanation: The passage gives a progression from cleansing and turning away from evil to doing good and seeking justice.
medium.q: What order of repentance is presented in these verses?

answers: Help the person who has been wronged
Give wealth to a powerful person
medium.explanation: The command calls for helping and defending those who are oppressed.

answers: They shall become white as snow or wool
They will be hidden from the people
medium.explanation: The Lord promises that scarlet and crimson sins can become white as snow and wool.
medium.q: What does the Lord promise concerning sins that are as scarlet?

answers: It replaces every form of judgment
challenge.explanation: Repentance is shown not only in words but also in doing justice for the vulnerable.
challenge.q: How is defending the fatherless and widow connected with repentance?

answers: Between living in a city and living in a village
challenge.explanation: The people must choose between obedience, which brings the land’s goodness, and rebellion, which brings the sword.
challenge.q: What choice is presented in verses 19–20?

answers: Forgiveness is presented as part of repentance and moral reform
Forgiveness is given regardless of conduct
Doing good removes the possibility of forgiveness
challenge.explanation: The passage connects cleansing and forgiveness with turning from evil and practicing justice.
challenge.q: How does the promise of cleansed sins relate to the command to do good?

paragraphs.title: Corrupt Jerusalem and the Need for Purification

answers: As a faithful city full of judgment
easy.explanation: Jerusalem was once called “the faithful city” where righteousness lodged.
easy.q: How is Jerusalem described in the past?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “Thy silver is become dross.”

answers: They did not judge the fatherless or hear the widow’s cause
They did not give them land
They did not invite them to a feast
easy.explanation: The princes neglected justice for the fatherless and the widow.
easy.q: What did the princes fail to do for the fatherless and widow?

answers: Rebellion, bribery, and neglect of the vulnerable
medium.explanation: The rulers were rebellious, loved gifts, followed rewards, and neglected the weak.
medium.q: What caused the faithful city to become corrupt?

medium.explanation: Dross is refuse or impurity in metal, symbolizing moral corruption.
The Lord promises to restore the judges and counselors as they were at the beginning.
medium.q: What will the Lord do to restore Jerusalem?

answers: The city lost its purity and moral worth
challenge.explanation: The image describes the corruption of something that should have been pure and valuable.
challenge.q: What does the image of silver becoming dross teach about Jerusalem?

answers: Purification includes correcting the city’s leadership
The judges alone caused the dross
challenge.explanation: Jerusalem’s purification includes replacing corrupt leadership with righteous leadership.
challenge.q: How is the purging of dross related to the restoration of judges and counselors?

answers: The city of righteousness, the faithful city
challenge.explanation: After judgment and restoration, Jerusalem will be called “The city of righteousness, the faithful city.”
challenge.q: What will Jerusalem be called after its restoration?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “Zion shall be redeemed with judgment, and her converts with righteousness.”
easy.q: By what shall Zion be redeemed?

easy.explanation: The transgressors and those who forsake the Lord shall be destroyed or consumed.
easy.q: What will happen to transgressors and those who forsake the Lord?

answers: A withering oak and a garden without water
easy.explanation: They are compared to an oak whose leaf fades and a garden without water.
easy.q: What will the sinners be like?

answers: The oaks and gardens they desired and chose
medium.explanation: They will be ashamed of the oaks and gardens in which they delighted.
medium.q: What will cause the sinners to be ashamed?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes a tree losing its vitality and drying up.

answers: Dryness, weakness, and loss of life
medium.explanation: A garden without water becomes dry and lifeless.
medium.q: What does a garden without water symbolize?

answers: Zion is redeemed through judgment and righteousness, while the transgressors are consumed
They all receive the same outcome
Zion is destroyed while the transgressors are saved
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts Zion’s redemption with the destruction of sinners and those who forsake the Lord.
challenge.q: How are Zion and the transgressors distinguished in these verses?

answers: What they chose and desired becomes a source of shame and destruction
The oaks and gardens save them from the fire
challenge.explanation: The objects of their desire become associated with shame, dryness, and final burning.
challenge.q: How are the desired oaks and gardens connected with the fire at the end?

answers: The severity and unstoppable nature of the judgment
The abundance of water in the land
challenge.explanation: A fire that none can quench emphasizes the seriousness and finality of the destruction.
challenge.q: What does the image of an unquenchable fire emphasize?
